title: Putting a Peg in a Hole: A Chamfer, a Friction Cone, and a Hand That Gives Sideways So the Peg Can Find the Hole

questions.question: What gives the peg a sideways force on a chamfer?
options: The clearance between the peg and the hole
The push down on a slope, less friction
questions.explanation: A push straight down onto a slope has a part along the slope. Friction takes some of it, and the rest moves the peg toward the hole.

questions.question: A peg 2 mm off needed what push from a hand of 300 N/m?
questions.explanation: The stiffness times the distance the peg has to move, over the tangent of the slope less the friction. The softer the hand, the less push.

questions.question: The stiff hand (100000 N/m) at that offset:
options: Got it in, with all of its 50 N
Missed the chamfer and landed on the flat
questions.explanation: It would have needed 279 N to be pushed 2 mm sideways and had 50. The peg sat on the slope and went nowhere.

questions.question: At a friction of 1.2 on a 45 degree chamfer can the peg slide?
options: Yes, if the hand is soft enough
Yes, with a push of more than 279 N
Only if the peg lands near the bottom of the chamfer
questions.explanation: The tangent of 45 degrees is 1, less than the friction of 1.2. The slope is inside the friction cone, and pushing harder only presses harder.

questions.question: What helps a peg that cannot slide?
options: A steeper chamfer or less friction
A larger clearance in the hole
questions.explanation: The sideways force is the push times the tangent less the friction. When that is zero or less, only changing the angle or the friction makes it positive.

questions.question: What is not in this model?
options: The wedge: the peg touching at two points
The sideways stiffness of the hand
questions.explanation: The model stops when the peg is over the hole. A peg part way in that tilts and touches at two points is a different failure.
